match.reason: No single bank point teaches both halves of this brief: his-judging-historical-significance covers significance but not differing interpretations of the same evidence, and his-historical-interpretations covers interpretation but not judging significance by effects, so neither fits as it is or with small changes.

note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Question a, wording: Two distractors use absolutes ('must have used fake or forged sources', 'Only one historian can read') and a third says 'no evidence at all'. The card says historians 'can' or 'may' differ, so a student can rule out these options from the absolute wording alone and pick the right answer without knowing the idea.

rejected.title: Significance and interpretation
card: Significance is how much an event, person or change mattered. Historians judge it by its effects at the time and later.
Effects can be judged by how many people were affected, how deeply their lives changed and how long the effects lasted.
An interpretation is a historian's explanation of the past, built from evidence.
Historians can reach different interpretations from the same evidence. They may ask different questions, weigh sources differently or judge significance differently.
rejected.remember: Significance is judged by effects. Different interpretations can come from the same evidence.

a.q: Two historians study the same sources on the Black Death but reach different interpretations. What is the most likely reason?
opts: They weighed sources differently or asked other questions
One of them must have used fake or forged sources
Interpretations are guesses that need no evidence at all
Only one historian can read the same evidence properly
a.why: Historians can read the same evidence and stress different parts of it, or ask different questions of it. The tempting wrong answer says one must have used fake sources, but a difference in interpretation does not mean a source is fake.
a.clue: Think about what historians do with the same evidence.

b.q: A railway reaches a small town in 1880. Within ten years, its farmers sell crops far away, and the town grows and stays larger for a century. Why might a historian call the railway significant?
opts: Its effects reached many people and lasted a long time
It was new to the town and people talked about it
It happened long ago and is recorded in old sources
It was costly to build and took years to finish
b.why: Significance is judged by effects: how many people they reached, how deep they were and how long they lasted. Here the railway changed farming and growth for a century. Being new or talked about does not make something significant if its effects are small.
b.clue: Look at what happened to the town after the railway came.

a.q: Two historians study the same sources on the Black Death but reach different interpretations. What is the most likely reason?
opts: They weighed the evidence or asked different questions
One of them must have used fake sources
Interpretations are only guesses with no evidence
Only one historian can use the evidence properly
a.why: Historians can read the same evidence and stress different parts of it, or ask different questions of it. The tempting wrong answer says one must be wrong, but a difference in interpretation does not mean a source is fake.
a.clue: Think about what historians do with the same evidence.

b.q: A railway reaches a small town in 1880. Within ten years, its farmers sell crops far away, and the town grows and stays larger for a century. Why might a historian call the railway significant?
opts: It changed many lives and its effects lasted a long time
It was built in the year 1880
It was a new thing that people noticed
It was the only change in the town
b.why: Significance is judged by effects, including how widespread, deep and lasting they were. Here the railway changed farming and growth for a century. Being new or noticed does not make something significant if its effects are small.
b.clue: Look at what happened to the town after the railway came.
